PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT		§		PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION		§
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561		§		OF TEXAS

INITIAL COMMENTS OF CROW HOLDINGS
I.	Introduction
Crow Holdings respectfully submits these initial comments in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (“Commission”) proposed rulemaking under Project No. 58481, implementing Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561 and establishing Large Load Interconnection Standards, as codified in proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.194.
Crow Holdings wishes to begin by acknowledging the extraordinary scope and complexity of the undertaking reflected in this rulemaking. The Commission’s proposal reflects a genuine commitment to modernizing the large load interconnection process in a manner that is technically sound and equitable to market participants. Crow Holdings is grateful for that engagement and offers these comments in the same collaborative spirit.
Crow Holdings’ comments are narrowly focused on a single issue that, in our view, respectfully requires attention before the proposed rule is finalized: the treatment of large load interconnection requests that have already completed the full legacy interconnection study process, executed binding interconnection agreements, and posted substantial financial security to fund all required interconnection facilities. We believe that a targeted adjustment to proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 would resolve this issue in a manner fully consistent with the Commission’s reliability objectives under PURA § 37.0561, while honoring the commitments that market participants have already made in good faith under the legacy framework. We recognize the Commission’s desire to distinguish legitimate large load developments from proposed projects that may be on the more speculative end of the spectrum. However, we caution against creating a framework that penalizes genuine large load developers with considerable commitments who have full control of their site, as doing so would materially jeopardize the State’s reputation and competitiveness as a destination for investment. Finally, we ask that the Commission continue to provide clarity on the framework changes, such that committed developers can continue to invest in the State with confidence.
II.	Background and the Need to Honor Prior Commitments
The Commission’s proposed rule establishes new interconnection standards applicable to large load customers, including new financial security requirements, site control demonstrations, and agreement structures. The rule is designed to address the significant influx of large load interconnection requests and to transition toward a structured, coordinated study framework.
The proposed rule, however, does not expressly address how it applies to large loads that have already completed the prior interconnection study process in its entirety—including obtaining all required determinations of transmission facilities needed for interconnection, executing binding interconnection agreements or equivalent service extension agreements with the applicable Transmission Service Provider(s) (“TSPs”), and posting all financial security required to fund the interconnection facilities identified in the completed studies.
These large load customers have satisfied every substantive obligation that the legacy framework required of them. They have demonstrated project seriousness, financial capability, and commitments to specific, studied interconnection configurations. Subjecting these projects to re-evaluation under new rule provisions—or requiring them to execute new or amended interconnection agreements—would impose material burdens that are inconsistent with the investments and commitments these customers have already made, and that are not necessary to achieve the Commission’s reliability and cost-protection objectives. Furthermore, changing the rules midstream is inconsistent with our previous experiences in Texas and the introduced uncertainty is damaging to the State’s economic development objectives and reputation as an investable, pro-business state.
III.	Proposed Addition to 16 TAC § 25.194: Honoring Prior Commitments of Fully Committed Legacy Projects
Crow Holdings recommends that the Commission include a provision within proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 that honors the prior commitments of large load customers that have fully satisfied the obligations of the legacy large load interconnection study (“LLIS”) process. Specifically, any large load customer that meets the following criteria should not be subject to further evaluation under any new or restudied interconnection process, or to any requirement to execute a new or amended interconnection agreement:
The large load customer has executed a binding interconnection agreement or equivalent service extension agreement with the interconnecting TSP and, if different from the interconnecting TSP, the interconnecting DSP; and
The interconnecting TSP and, if different from the interconnecting TSP, the interconnecting DSP have received from the large load customer the financial security, applicable payments, and/or other agreements required to fund all necessary interconnection facilities identified in the completed interconnection studies.
The large load customer has demonstrated full site control by holding fee title, or executed lease of duration the Commission deems sufficient to the proposed load location.
The large load customer has demonstrated project advancement by placing reasonable and necessary long lead equipment deposits or made other financial commitments and has issued a purchase order or similar order commitment.

IV.	Rationale: Why the Commission Should Honor Prior Commitments
A.	Fully Committed Projects Present No Speculative Risk
The Commission’s core objective in adopting new interconnection standards is to screen out speculative, non-viable projects that consume study resources and complicate transmission planning without offering meaningful certainty of interconnection. That concern is entirely legitimate and well-founded.
However, a large load customer that has completed the LLIS process, executed a binding interconnection agreement, and posted financial security sufficient to fund all identified interconnection facilities is, by definition, not speculative. Such a customer has already passed through the full substantive screening process the legacy framework provides. The transmission impacts of the project have been studied, the needed facilities have been identified, and the customer has made binding financial commitments to fund those facilities. Requiring these customers to re-enter a new study process, or to execute new or amended interconnection agreements, adds no screening value and imposes real harm on participants who have acted in reasonable reliance on the rules as they existed.
B.	Consistency with PURA § 37.0561
PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. Honoring prior commitments serves all three of these statutory goals.
First, protecting the interconnection rights of committed customers supports business development by providing certainty that substantial capital investments in interconnection agreements will not be rendered worthless by a change in regulatory framework.
Second, honoring the prior commitments of fully committed legacy projects minimizes the risk of stranded costs. These customers have already funded or committed to fund the specific facilities needed to serve their load. Disrupting those commitments could leave funded infrastructure in limbo, increasing rather than reducing the risk of stranded investment.
Third, grid reliability is not compromised by protecting legacy projects that have undergone complete interconnection studies. To the contrary, the transmission facilities those studies identified—and which the customers have committed to fund—support system reliability by ensuring that load additions are served through studied and approved configurations.
C.	The Proposed Provision Is Narrowly and Appropriately Tailored
The proposed provision is not a broad exemption from new requirements. It applies only to large loads that have satisfied both of the following demanding criteria: (1) execution of a binding interconnection agreement or equivalent service extension agreement; and (2) delivery of all financial security required to fund the facilities identified in completed interconnection studies. These criteria are demanding. Not every large load customer with a pending request will satisfy them. Only those customers who have completed the full legacy process and made binding financial commitments will qualify.
This narrow scope ensures that the proposed protection is limited to the precise category of projects for which re-evaluation would be most inequitable and least productive, while preserving the Commission’s full authority to apply new interconnection standards to all other large load customers.
D.	Failure to Honor Prior Commitments Creates Unjust and Retroactive Regulatory Consequences
Large load customers that completed the LLIS process and executed binding interconnection agreements did so in reliance on the regulatory framework as it existed at the time. They made significant financial commitments—including the posting of financial security to fund specific, studied transmission facilities—based on expectations that their interconnection rights would be honored.
Applying new rule requirements to these customers retroactively—requiring them to re-enter a study process, post additional financial security, or execute new interconnection agreements—would impose obligations that were not in existence when the customers made their commitments and that are not necessary to address the concerns the new rule is designed to resolve. Such an outcome is inconsistent with fundamental principles of regulatory fairness and would undermine confidence in the stability and predictability of the interconnection process.
E.	Demonstrated Site Control in Fee Ownership and Long Lead Equipment Purchase Order Provides Independent and Conclusive Evidence of Project Legitimacy and Advancement
The Commission’s proposed rule correctly identifies site control as a threshold indicator of project seriousness and viability. Proposed §25.194(d)(1) requires large load customers to demonstrate site control as a precondition to entering the interconnection process precisely because ownership or a committed property interest at the proposed load location is among the most reliable signals that a project is genuine rather than speculative.
Crow Holdings respectfully submits that where a large load customer has demonstrated site control through outright ownership of the proposed load location in fee or executed lease of duration the Commission deems sufficient, that demonstration, combined with a completed LLIS, executed interconnection agreement, and posted financial security, constitutes conclusive evidence that the project is not of the speculative character the new framework is designed to screen out. Additionally, as a demonstration of meaningful project advancement, we submit that where a large load customer has made financial commitments to long lead equipment reasonable and necessary for the project, this is sufficient to prove conclusive evidence of customer commitment.

A customer that owns or has leased the land, has completed the interconnection study, executed a binding agreement with the utility, posted financial security, and begun the long lead equipment purchase  process has taken the necessary steps to legitimize a project. 

V.	Proposed Rule Language
To address the concerns identified above, Crow Holdings recommends that the Commission include the following provision within proposed 16 TAC § 25.194, either as a new subsection or as an express carve-out from provisions governing study and agreement requirements:

Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, a large load customer that meets the following requirements shall not be subject to further evaluation under any new interconnection study process, or to any requirement to execute a new or amended interconnection agreement, pursuant to this section:
(i) The large load customer has executed a binding interconnection agreement or equivalent service extension agreement with the interconnecting TSP and, if different from the interconnecting TSP, the interconnecting DSP; and
(ii) The interconnecting TSP and, if different from the interconnecting TSP, the interconnecting DSP have received from the large load customer the financial security, applicable payments, and/or other agreements required to fund all necessary interconnection facilities identified in the completed interconnection studies.; and
(iii) The large load customer has demonstrated full site control by holding fee title to the proposed load location, or executed lease of duration the Commission deems sufficient; and
(iv) The large load customer has demonstrated project advancement by placing reasonable and necessary long lead equipment deposits or made other financial commitments and has issued a purchase order or similar order commitment.


VI.	Conclusion
Crow Holdings supports the Commission’s efforts to modernize the large load interconnection process and establish a durable framework capable of managing the scale and complexity of large load development in Texas. The transition to a structured, coordinated study process, combined with meaningful financial commitment requirements, represents a constructive and necessary evolution in transmission planning.
At the same time, the Commission should ensure that the new framework does not impose retroactive burdens on large load customers that have already completed the legacy interconnection study process, executed binding interconnection agreements, and posted all required financial security while controlling the land and demonstrating real site advancement. These customers have demonstrated precisely the level of commitment and project viability that the new framework is designed to require. Honoring their prior commitments through a targeted, narrowly drawn provision is consistent with PURA § 37.0561, equitable to market participants who have acted in reliance on the prior framework, and consistent with the Commission’s reliability and cost-protection objectives.
Crow Holdings respectfully requests that the Commission incorporate the proposed provision honoring prior commitments into 16 TAC § 25.194 as described above.


Respectfully submitted,


Kevin McMeans
Crow Holdings
3819 Maple Avenue
Dallas, TX 75219
214-922-8406
Kmcmeans@crowholdings.com
